glossary.Campylobacter jejuni: A common bacterial cause of food poisoning, often from undercooked chicken or raw milk, causing bloody diarrhoea.
glossary.Staphylococcus aureus: A common bacterium that can grow in food and release a toxin causing rapid vomiting.
glossary.Giardia lamblia: A single-celled parasite spread in contaminated water that causes watery diarrhoea, bloating and malabsorption.
glossary.Giardiasis: Infection of the small bowel with the parasite Giardia lamblia.
glossary.enteric: Relating to the intestines; enteric fever is another name for typhoid.
glossary.stepwise fever: A fever that rises a little higher each day, typical of typhoid.
glossary.unpasteurised: Not heat-treated to kill bacteria, so raw milk or cheese can carry infection.
glossary.immunosuppression: A weakened immune system, from disease or drugs, making infections more likely and more severe.
glossary.immunocompromise: A reduced ability of the immune system to fight infection.
glossary.cephalosporins: A family of broad-spectrum antibiotics, such as ceftriaxone, that raise the risk of C. difficile.
glossary.ciprofloxacin: A quinolone antibiotic; broad-spectrum use raises the risk of C. difficile infection.
glossary.penicillins: A family of antibiotics, such as amoxicillin, that can disturb gut bacteria and allow C. difficile to grow.
glossary.stool culture: Growing bacteria from a faecal sample in the lab to identify the organism.
glossary.stool microscopy: Looking at a faecal sample under the microscope for parasites, cysts or ova.
glossary.blood culture: Blood placed in bottles to grow any bacteria present; the test for typhoid.
glossary.FBC: Full blood count: haemoglobin, white cells and platelets.
glossary.prodrome: Early non-specific symptoms, such as feeling flu-like, before the main illness starts.
glossary.plaques: Raised, flat-topped patches on a surface, here yellow patches on the bowel lining.
glossary.sanitation: Clean water supply and safe disposal of sewage.
glossary.septic: Having sepsis: a life-threatening body-wide response to infection causing organ dysfunction.
glossary.electrolyte: Salts in the blood such as sodium and potassium, lost in diarrhoea and vomiting.
glossary.dehydration: Loss of more body water than is taken in, causing thirst, dry mouth, low urine output and low BP.
glossary.0.9% saline: Normal saline: the standard intravenous salt-water fluid used for rehydration.
glossary.IV: Intravenous: given directly into a vein.
glossary.relapse: Return of the illness after it had got better.
glossary.isolation: Nursing an infectious patient in a single room to stop spread to others.
glossary.hand hygiene: Hand washing; soap and water is needed for C. difficile because alcohol gel does not kill its spores.
glossary.infection control: Measures such as hand washing and isolation that stop infections spreading in hospital.
glossary.mucosa: The inner lining of the gut.
glossary.disseminates: Spreads from the original site around the body.
glossary.myelin: The fatty insulating sheath around nerve fibres that speeds up nerve signals.
glossary.peripheral nerve: A nerve outside the brain and spinal cord.
glossary.heat-stable: Not destroyed by cooking, so reheating contaminated food does not make it safe.
glossary.toxins A and B: The two toxins made by C. difficile that damage the colon lining.
glossary.cytoskeleton: The internal protein scaffold that holds a cell's shape and its junctions together.
glossary.epithelial: Relating to the layer of cells lining a surface, such as the inside of the colon.
glossary.pathogens: Organisms that cause disease, such as bacteria, viruses and parasites.
glossary.bloating: A feeling of fullness and swelling in the abdomen, often from gas.
